source_text:
At tamen ista ipsa superstitio Eomanis dedit, auxit, fundauit imperium, cum non tam uirtute quam religione et pietate pollerent. nimirum insignis et nobilis iustitia Romana ab ipsis imperii nascentis incunabulis auspicata est.
nonne in ortu suo et scelere: collecti et muniti immanitatis suae terrore creuerunt? nam asylo prima plebs congregata est: confluxerant perditi, facinerosi, incesti, sicarii, proditores, et ut ipse Romulus imperator et rector populum suum facinore praecelleret, parricidium fecit. haec prima sunt auspicia religiosae ciuitatis.
mox alienas uirgines iam desponsatas, iam destinatas et nonnullas de matrimonio mulierculas sine more rapuit, uiolauit, inlusit, et cum earum parentibus, id est cum soceris suis bellum miscuit, propinquum sanguinem fudit. quid inreligiosius, quid audacius, quid ipsa sceleris confidentia turpius ?
iam finitimos agro pellere, ciuitates proximas euertere cum templis et altaribus, captos cogere, damnis alienis et suis sceleribus adolescere cum Romulo regibus ceteris et posteris ducibus disciplina communis est.
ita quicquid Romani tenent, colunt, possident, audaciae praeda est: templa omnia de manubiis, id est de ruinis urbium, de spoliis deorum, de caedibus sacerdotum: hoc insultare et inludere est, uictis religionibus seruire, captiuas eas post uictorias adorare. nam adorare quae manu ceperis, sacrilegium est consecrare, non numina.
totiens ergo Romanis inpiatum est quotiens triumphatum, tot de diis spolia quot de gentibus sunt tropaea. igitur Romani non ideo tanti, quod religiosi, sed quod inpune sacrilegi.
neque enim potuerunt in ipsis bellis deos adiutores habere, aduersus quos arma rapuerunt, sed quos prostrauerant, detriumphatos colere coeperunt. quid autem isti dii pro Romanis possunt, qui nihil pro suis aduersus eorum arma ualuerunt? Romanorum enim uernaculos deos nouimus: Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus et Consus et Pilumnus ac Volumnus dii.
Cloacinam Tatius et inuenit et coluit, Pauorem Hostilius atque Pallorem, mox a nescio quo Febris dedicata: haec alumna urbis istius superstitio, morbi et malae ualetudines. sane et Acca Larentia et Flora, meretrices propudiosae, inter morbos Romanorum et deos computandae.
isti scilicet aduersus ceteros, qui in gentibus colebantur, Romanorum imperium protulerunt: neque enim eos aduersum suos homines uel Mars Thracius uel Iuppiter Creticus uel Iuno nunc Argiua, nunc Samia, nunc Poena, uel Diana Taurica uel Mater Idaea uel Aegyptia illa non numina, sed portenta uuerunt.
nisi forte apud istos maior castitas uirginum aut religio sanctior sacerdotum, cum paene in pluribus uirginibus, set quae inconsultius se uiris miscuissent, Vesta sane nesciente, sit incestum uindicatum, in residuis inpunitatem fecerit non castitas tutior, sed inpudicitia felicior.
ubi autem magis a sacerdotibus quam inter aras et delubra conducuntur stupra, tractantur lenocinia, adulteria meditantur ? frequentius denique in aedituorum cellulis quam m ipsis lupanaribus flagrans libido defungitur.
et tamen ante eos Deo dispensante diu regna tenuerunt Assyrii, Medi, Persae, Graeci etiam et Aegyptii, cum Pontifices et Aruales et Salios et Vestales et Augures non haberent nec pullos cauea reclusos, quorum cibo uel fastidio res publica summa regeretur.
thought_title: Rome's greatness came from crime, not religion
orientation: Caecilius is still speaking, attacking the claim that Roman power rests on traditional worship by arguing that Rome grew through sacrilege and that its gods are worthless.
pass_a_gloss: And yet this very superstition gave, increased, founded the Roman empire, since they were strong not so much by virtue as by religion and piety. To be sure, the famous and noble Roman justice was inaugurated from the very cradle of the nascent empire. Did they not in their origin both by crime: gathered and fortified, they grew by the terror of their savagery? For the first common people was gathered in an asylum: the ruined, the criminal, the incestuous, the assassins, the traitors had flowed together, and so that Romulus himself, as commander and ruler, might surpass his own people in crime, he committed parricide. These are the first auspices of the religious city. Soon he seized foreign maidens already betrothed, already promised, and some little women from marriage without custom, violated them, mocked them, and with their parents, that is with his own fathers-in-law, he mixed war, he shed kindred blood. What is more irreligious, what more reckless, what more shameful than the very confidence of crime? Now to drive neighbors from their land, to overturn nearby cities with temples and altars, to force captives, to grow by others' losses and their own crimes was common discipline with Romulus, the other kings, and later leaders. Thus whatever the Romans hold, worship, possess, is the booty of recklessness: all temples from spoils, that is from the ruins of cities, from the spoils of gods, from the slaughters of priests: this is to insult and mock, to enslave conquered religions, to adore them as captives after victories. For to adore what you have taken by hand is sacrilege to consecrate, not deities. Therefore the Romans acted impiously as often as they triumphed, there are as many spoils from gods as there are trophies from nations. Therefore the Romans are not so great because they are religious, but because they are sacrilegious with impunity. For they could not have had gods as helpers in those very wars, against whom they took up arms, but those whom they had laid low, they began to worship as triumphed-over. But what can these gods do for the Romans, who had no power for their own people against their arms? For we know the home-born gods of the Romans: Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus and Consus and Pilumnus and Volumnus are gods. Tatius both found and worshipped Cloacina, Hostilius Fear and Pallor, soon Fever was dedicated by someone unknown: these are the nurslings of this city, superstition, diseases and bad states of health. Indeed also Acca Larentia and Flora, shameless prostitutes, are to be counted among the diseases and gods of the Romans. These, of course, advanced the Roman empire against the others who were worshipped among the nations: for neither Thracian Mars nor Cretan Jupiter nor Juno now Argive, now Samian, now Carthaginian, nor Tauric Diana nor the Idaean Mother nor those Egyptian things, not deities but monsters, had power against their own people. Unless perhaps among these there is greater chastity of virgins or holier religion of priests, when in almost more virgins, but those who had mixed themselves with men too thoughtlessly, Vesta of course not knowing, incest was punished, in the rest impunity made not chastity safer, but shamelessness luckier. But where more are rapes contracted by priests than among altars and shrines, pimping is handled, adulteries are planned? More frequently, in fact, burning lust is finished off in the cells of temple-keepers than in the brothels themselves. And yet before them, by God's dispensation, the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Greeks also and Egyptians held kingdoms for a long time, although they did not have Pontiffs and Arval Brothers and Salii and Vestals and Augurs, nor chickens shut in a cage, by whose food or distaste the highest state was ruled.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for false or excessive religious practice; Caecilius is ironically conceding the term Octavius would use.
Caecilius is quoting the traditional Roman claim; religio is the glossary term for proper worship, and pietas is rendered literally as piety to preserve the paired Roman virtues.
Glossary term sacrilege for violation of what is sacred; the infinitive consecrare keeps the paradoxical force of consecrating captured gods.
The adverb inpune is key to Caecilius's point that Rome's success is not proof of divine favor but of unpunished sacrilege.
Numen is the glossary term for divine power; portenta as monsters preserves the contrast between true divine power and monstrous foreign cult objects.
Glossary term incest for alleged sexual immorality; here Caecilius uses it of Vestal virgins, and uindicatum as punished keeps the legal force.

pass_b_english: And yet this very superstition gave Rome its empire, enlarged it, and established it, since they were strong not so much by virtue as by religion and piety. Indeed, the famous and noble justice of Rome began from the very cradle of the rising empire.

Did they not grow from their origin in crime, gathered together and protected by the terror of their own savagery? For the first crowd was assembled in an asylum: the lost, the criminal, the incestuous, murderers, traitors had flocked there, and so that Romulus himself, their commander and ruler, might surpass his people in crime, he committed parricide. These are the first beginnings of the religious city.

Soon he seized, violated, and mocked foreign maidens already betrothed, already promised, and some married women, without any custom, and he stirred up war with their parents, that is, with his own fathers-in-law, and shed kindred blood. What is more irreligious, what is more reckless, what is more shameful than the very boldness of the crime?

Then to drive neighbors from their land, to overthrow nearby cities with their temples and altars, to force captives into bondage, to grow by the losses of others and by their own crimes: this has been the common practice of Romulus, the other kings, and the leaders who followed.

So whatever the Romans hold, worship, and possess is the plunder of their audacity: all their temples come from spoils, that is, from the ruins of cities, from the plunder of gods, from the slaughter of priests. This is to insult and mock: to enslave conquered religions and to worship them as captives after victories. For to worship what you have seized by force is sacrilege to consecrate, not deities.

Therefore the Romans have acted impiously as often as they have triumphed, and they have taken as many spoils from the gods as they have trophies from the nations. So the Romans are great not because they are religious, but because they are sacrilegious with impunity.

For they could not have had the gods as helpers in those very wars against whom they took up arms, but after overthrowing them, they began to worship the gods they had triumphed over. What can these gods do for the Romans, when they had no power for their own people against Roman arms? For we know the home-born gods of the Romans: Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus, and Consus, and Pilumnus and Volumnus are gods.

Tatius both discovered and worshipped Cloacina, the goddess of the sewer. Hostilius dedicated Panic and Pallor, the gods of terror and fear, and soon Fever was dedicated by someone or other: this is the foster-child of that city, superstition, diseases and bad health. Indeed, Acca Larentia and Flora, shameless prostitutes, must be counted among the diseases and gods of the Romans.

These, of course, extended the Roman empire against the others who were worshipped among the nations: for neither Thracian Mars nor Cretan Jupiter nor Juno, now Argive, now Samian, now Carthaginian, nor Tauric Diana nor the Idaean Mother nor those Egyptian nothings, not deities but portents, helped their own people against Roman arms.

Unless perhaps among these there is greater chastity of virgins or holier religion of priests, when in nearly the majority of virgins, but those who had mingled with men too thoughtlessly, Vesta surely not knowing, incest was punished, while in the rest impunity did not make chastity safer, but made shamelessness more fortunate.

Where, moreover, are debaucheries hired out, pimping conducted, adulteries plotted more by priests than among altars and shrines? Finally, burning lust is satisfied more often in the cells of temple keepers than in the brothels themselves.

And yet before them, by God's dispensation, the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Greeks, and even Egyptians held kingdoms for a long time, though they had no Pontiffs, Arval Brothers, Salii, Vestals, or Augurs, nor sacred chickens shut in a cage, by whose appetite or disgust the highest affairs of state were governed.
notes: Source has 'Eomanis' for 'Romanis' and 'm ipsis' for 'in ipsis' and 'nenio' for 'uenio' in the following section; these appear to be OCR errors. The gloss renders the intended words.
Source has 'set' for 'sed' in 'set quae inconsultius'.

problems.ruling: 'Pauorem' is a deity of panic/terror, not 'the Poor'; translation misidentifies deity.

The source reads 'nec pullos cauea reclusos, quorum cibo uel fastidio res publica summa regeretur'. The English is accurate; no edit needed.

Earlier edit: 'since they lacked religion and piety more than virtue' - the source reads 'cum non tam uirtute quam religione et pietate pollerent', meaning 'since they were strong not so much by virtue as by religion and piety'. The earlier edit was wrong; corrected.
